newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Hopes fade for survivors in Australian landslide.
newsitem.headline: Hopes fade for survivors in Australian landslide.

text.p: Up to 20 people were feared killed or injured after a landslide demolished two lodges in Australia's Snowy Mountains, police said on Thursday, as rescuers searched for survivors under the threat of more landslides.
The rescue operation at Thredbo, Australia's most popular ski resort, might take up to two days because the site was still dangerously unstable, police said.

Police said about 20 people were inside the Carinya and Bimbadeen lodges when the landslide occurred just before midnight on Wednesday at the Thredbo Alpine Village in the Snowy Mountains, 150 km (90 miles) southwest of Canberra.
Rescue operations in the freezing temperatures were delayed about 10 hours because of fears of more landslides, and police at the scene said the situation looked grim.
Regional police commander Bruce Johnston said the chances of finding survivors was fading.
"The longer it goes, obviously their chances are diminishing," he told reporters.
Johnston said the rescue was a dangerous operation, with geologists warning that more slides were virtually inevitable.
Rescuers remained hopeful of finding someone alive in the tonnes of rubble, but no voices had been heard from the wreckage since soon after the landslide.
"We do hold some hopes that there may be survivors," Johnston said, but added: "We haven't heard any sounds or been given any physical signs there are survivors."
Most of the missing are Thredbo Alpine Resort staff.
Resort managing director David Osborn said the missing workers were men and women aged between 25 and 50 and some were foreigners, including Americans.
Rescuers were removing debris largely by hand and shoring up the wreckage as they went. "It's such a delicate operation," Johnston said.
Despite the freezing temperatures, an ambulance official said people could still be alive if they lived through the initial impact.

"There could be a chance that they have survived and considering they were wrapped in their blankets they would be warm and you wouldn't rule out the chance of finding someone alive," ambulance official Graeme Field told Reuters.
Heat-imaging equipment has been brought in to search for survivors.
Eyewitnesses said the landslide sounded like a big gust of wind that shook the lodges perched on the side of the mountain.
"We just heard this enormous rush like I'd imagine you'd experience with a tornado just hitting a building...," said Glenn Milne, who was holidaying in an adjacent lodge.
The landslide occurred just before midnight at a time when Thredbo, at an altitude of 1,370 metres (4,494 feet), was packed with thousands of Australian and foreign visitors.
Thredbo sits on a ridge facing the snow-covered mountain range of the Kosciuszko National Park, which rises to 2,037 metres (6,683 feet).
Australia's ski season runs from June to October, but a poor start to the season has seen little snow fall on the village.
Police believe seepage from a mountain spring may have caused the earth to give way, sending tonnes of dirt, rock and gum trees crashing onto the lodges.
"It looks like someone has taken a great big bulldozer and just drove over both the lodges and they just slid down the hill," one unidentified witness told reporters.
"It reminds me of looking at a picture of a tornado site or something where it's just cleaned a path through and on either side there is no damage whatsoever," he said.
